en.summary: Everyday neighbourhood life right outside the MRT station: a wet market, breakfast stalls, coffee and cooked food under one roof. A good first stop on a Clementi route. Watch how residents shop for groceries and eat breakfast, then pick one or two stalls to try. The centre is one place; check each stall's opening hours separately.
en.fun_fact: One centre brings together different food traditions, from Hainanese porridge to oyster omelette. Diners on Burpple point to Soon Lee porridge at #01-50 and Fu Xiang oyster omelette at #01-09, which could later become their own stall cards.
en.hours: Each stall keeps its own hours; there are usually more options at breakfast and lunch. Check with the stall owners.
en.access_notes: Check cleaning days and stall rest days separately. The centre has no verified central ordering phone number; don't treat one stall's number as the number for the whole centre.
en.review_summary: A 2024 diner said Soon Lee's meatball and pig's liver porridge had generous toppings and well-seasoned meatballs. This is one person's experience of one stall and does not represent every stall in the centre.

en.summary: A Teochew temple tucked between West Coast HDB blocks and a hawker centre. Look at the roof ridge decorations, the courtyard and community worship. Pair it with Ayer Rajah Food Centre across the road to see migrant faith and everyday food together, rather than just taking photos of the building.
en.fun_fact: The National Heritage Board traces the temple's origins to 1918, when Teochew migrants built it in a fishing village. It later moved to West Coast. The current site also promotes both Chinese and English so younger generations can understand the traditions.
en.hours: Visiting hours are not confirmed on a public temple page; call before a daytime visit
en.price: Usually free to pray; donations are voluntary
en.access_notes: Keep quiet and don't photograph people while they pray. Ask staff before taking photos indoors or during rituals. Older visitor accounts and heritage sources give different years for the move; we follow the National Heritage Board's account.
en.review_summary: A 2018 visitor noted the temple sits in a residential area, and that the arched bridge in the courtyard and Teochew architectural details are worth a look. There are very few reviews and they are old, so treat this only as a hint.

en.summary: A multi-ethnic canteen in the West Coast neighbourhood. Indian rojak, biryani and local Chinese snacks are worth exploring stall by stall. Works well as a short route with Ang Chee Sia Ong Temple. If you need halal food, check each stall's certification.
en.fun_fact: HDB lists this hawker centre as the main draw of the Blocks 501–505 neighbourhood centre. In Singapore, a cultural spot can also be a market and canteen that serves residents.
en.hours: Each stall keeps its own hours; lunch and dinner options differ
en.access_notes: Don't assume the whole centre is halal. Some online directories list the phone number 11111111, which is clearly a placeholder and has not been used.
en.review_summary: Diners say there is a wide choice of Indian and Malay food. Other 2023–2024 reviews complained about service or drink prices at certain stalls. Ask the price before ordering at each stall, and don't take one stall's experience as true for the whole centre.

en.summary: A community mosque near Clementi MRT, easy to spot by its cream and brown boxy building. It is also a place for religious education, social services and neighbourhood activities. From the public areas, you can see how a modern mosque fits into an HDB town.
en.fun_fact: MUIS records that it was completed in 1989, holds about 3,000 worshippers and keeps a collection of Islamic texts. The mosque has also run computer classes for adults and children.
en.hours: Prayer times are not the same as visitor hours; non-worshippers should contact the mosque in advance
en.price: Free; ask in advance about guided tours
en.access_notes: Where and when non-Muslims may enter follows the mosque's instructions. Avoid Friday congregational prayers and dress modestly. Contact email: feedback@darussalam.mosque.org.sg.
en.review_summary: A 2018 visitor described the interior as quiet and close to the MRT and bus stops, and noted that non-Muslims have set visiting times. The review is old; for visitor arrangements, follow the mosque's latest reply.

en.summary: A hillside mosque on Clementi Road near NUS. Its minaret with a golden dome and its small-scale courtyard feel very different from the large religious buildings in the city centre. Fits well as an extension of an NUS Museum visit. Ask the mosque about visits before you go.
en.fun_fact: It was built in 1961 by Muslim members of the British forces. The name "Tentera Di Raja" honours the soldiers' contribution to building the mosque.
en.hours: Contact the mosque before visiting; prayer times are not the same as visitor hours
en.price: Free; ask in advance about guided tours
en.access_notes: The slope and steps may make access difficult; call first. It is in the outer Clementi area, so connect by bus. info@tentera.mosque.org.sg.
en.review_summary: A 2025 Google review shown on HHWT says the hillside setting is quiet with a kampung feel, and mentions that there are still steps to climb from the bus stop.

en.summary: View the rust-coloured truss bridge from the open path beside the Ulu Pandan canal. It is one of Clementi's most recognisable industrial relics. The thing to see is the bridge from outside and the canal view; this is not a walking route that uses the old bridge deck as a path.
en.fun_fact: The old Jurong Line once carried industrial freight. NParks includes the disused railway, tunnels, tracks and bridges in the history of the Clementi Nature Corridor, and records that the line stopped running in the early 1990s.
en.hours: View only from public paths open on site; daytime recommended
en.access_notes: The old bridge is not a way across the canal on this route. There is phased construction and diversions around the area; follow on-site fencing and the latest NParks notices. This card does not lead to the disused tracks or closed forest trails.
en.review_summary: A 2024 path user singled out the old truss bridge as a striking landmark along the way. The review is about the view from the path and does not show that the bridge deck is open.

en.summary: Walk slowly along the canal and look for herons, kingfishers, flowering trees and residents cycling or exercising in the morning. The full connector is about 14.8 km. This card only covers the stretch near Clementi and Sunset Way as a route stop; you don't need to walk the whole connector at once.
en.fun_fact: NParks highlights seasonal blooms here such as trumpet trees and pink kapok. The same urban drainage canal is also a place to watch grey herons and white-throated kingfishers hunting.
en.hours: Open stretches are generally open all day; lit 19:00–07:00. Daytime is best for birdwatching.
en.access_notes: The two banks are not always connected; don't cross the canal based on straight-line distance. Keep an eye on NParks diversion notices and follow the stretches open on site.
en.review_summary: A few visitors in 2024–2025 enjoyed the riverside views and how the walk links neighbourhoods. An older review mentioned a detour because of a landslide. Old reviews don't guarantee the whole route is open today.

en.summary: A wooded park beside West Coast Road. Shade, rolling ground and a small amphitheatre make it good for an easy walk. It is not the same place as Clementi Forest further north; don't mix up the two entrances because the names are similar.
en.fun_fact: The park covers about 12 hectares. Its amphitheatre in the woods puts everyday public events under the tree canopy. NParks has also set up community gardening facilities here.
en.hours: Open areas 24 hours; some areas under redevelopment
en.access_notes: NParks has announced partial redevelopment from 2025-09-15; use only open paths. Official listings mention accessibility features, but that doesn't guarantee every sloped path is passable.
en.review_summary: Visitors in 2017–2018 liked the quiet greenery and the rolling paths for walking and jogging. The reviews are old; check official updates for facilities and construction.

en.summary: A coastal park in the west for kite flying, family play and sunsets. Views towards the industrial port also bring out Singapore's "port city" theme. There is no long sandy beach like East Coast; the focus is lawns, playgrounds and the seaside path.
en.fun_fact: The 50-hectare park also has a small wetland area, the Marsh Garden. NParks suggests looking out for white-breasted waterhens and striated herons. Wildlife watching doesn't only happen in big nature reserves.
en.price: Free; parking and some activities cost extra
en.access_notes: Getting from Clementi station to the coast needs an extra walk or bus. The official map point on this card is not a single entrance to every facility.
en.review_summary: Family visitors in 2021–2022 liked the large playgrounds and fairly flat paths. Other visitors pointed out that the sea view has docks and containers in the background. Good facilities and a seaside holiday feel are different things.

en.summary: An old-school bakery on Sunset Way. Butter cream cake, chicken pie, cream horns and sugee cake give food culture a real taste. Buy a few items and learn, as you walk, about the links between local Hainanese baking and British and Eurasian pastries.
en.fun_fact: The shop dates back to 1965. Its name and range of cakes carry British influence, showing how local bakers turned European recipes into everyday HDB neighbourhood food.
en.hours: Listed on platforms as daily 09:00–20:00; not confirmed live by the shop. Ask about sell-outs and festive hours.
en.price: Depends on the pastry; prices in old articles are not current prices
en.access_notes: Pastries may sell out early. The phone number comes from public shop listings. Check the website and opening hours before you go.
en.review_summary: Diners in 2024–2025 liked the nostalgic butter cream cake and savoury pies; some found the pastry not flaky enough or too sweet. These are personal tastes; no full sentiment count was done.
